speaker: THERAPIST
text: Hello. I'm here to help. You don't need to rush—take your time if you'd like.

speaker: PATIENT
text: Uh. okay. I've been feeling really angry lately when things don't go my way. Like, if someone cuts me off in traffic or if my phone dies mid-conversation—it just. explodes inside me. I can't control it.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Anger like that can feel overwhelming. What happens right before you feel it start?

speaker: PATIENT
text: I. I get this tightness in my chest, like my heart's racing. My hands start shaking a little. And then—oh god—I feel like I'm going to explode. Like if someone touches me or says something wrong, it just. hits me all at once.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: That sounds intense. Does it feel like you're losing control?

speaker: PATIENT
text: Yeah. sometimes I do. Like, I want to scream or hit something. But then I think about what happens after—people get scared or mad at me. So I just. freeze. It's worse than the anger.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Freezing can be a way to protect yourself. What triggers it most?

speaker: PATIENT
text: Oh. when I'm with people who don't listen to me. Like my boss or my partner—if they interrupt or dismiss what I say, it's like a switch flips. And then. I just shut down. It's not even anger anymore; it's this numbness.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Numbness can be a way to avoid the pain of being hurt. Have you noticed patterns?

speaker: PATIENT
text: Yeah. it's worse when I'm tired or stressed from work. Like, if I've been on my feet all day, even a little pushback makes me snap. And then. I feel guilty after. Like I shouldn't be mad at them.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Guilt can make it harder to address the anger. What would help you feel safer?

speaker: PATIENT
text: I. I don't know. Maybe if I could just talk to someone without them judging me? Like, not in a big group—just one-on-one. Or maybe writing down what bothers me first before it gets too much.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Writing can be a great way to process. Would you like to try that here?

speaker: PATIENT
text: Uh. yeah? But I don't want to mess up. What if I say something wrong?

speaker: THERAPIST
text: No one's perfect. Just share what comes to mind—no need for perfection.

speaker: PATIENT
text: Okay. so if someone says something mean, I feel this rush in my chest and then—pause—I want to yell but freeze instead. Like, I'm not even mad at them; it's more like. I'm mad at myself for being so sensitive.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Self-blame can make it harder to heal. What would help you feel less alone?

speaker: PATIENT
text: I. don't know. Maybe if I could just listen to myself more? Like, when I'm angry, I feel like I'm not even me—just this big, loud thing inside me.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: That's a powerful feeling. Would you like to explore what that ‘me' inside feels like?

speaker: PATIENT
text: Yeah. but I don't want to cry or anything. It's just. scary how strong it gets. Like, if I try to calm down, it feels like I'm fighting something bigger than me.

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Fighting it can make it stronger. What if we try small steps?

speaker: PATIENT
text: Like. what? Just taking deep breaths when it starts?

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Or writing down one thing that triggers you before it gets too big.

speaker: PATIENT
text: Okay. but what if I still feel bad after? Like, what if it's not ‘fixed'?

speaker: THERAPIST
text: Healing isn't linear. What would help you feel less afraid of it?

speaker: PATIENT
text: I. don't know. Maybe if I could just try one thing and not worry about it failing? Like, even if it doesn't work—just. trying?

speaker: THERAPIST
text: That's brave. Would you like to practice that now?

speaker: PATIENT
text: Yeah. but I don't want to mess up. What if I say something wrong again?

speaker: THERAPIST
text: No mistakes—just learning. Let's start small.
